strengths: This paper introduces on a very important problem and gives some solid baselines to tackle it.
The method, error metrics, experimental settings, baselines, and evaluations are thoughtfully designed (in general).
the extra mile effort in deriving confidence intervals;
the use of dataset selection methods in experimental evaluations;
an analysis of why the confidence intervals are large around $p=1/2$;
the experimental setting of book copyright infringement;
Identifying the dataset used to train a Machine Learning model could have a direct impact on privacy rights or copyright infringement, as mentioned in the Introduction.
I also appreciate that their proposed procedure is cost-effective and intuitive.
there is a lot of merit in noticing that Member Identification methods suffer from biases and then presenting an straight-forward tool to address this issue.
This paper introduces a new task in privacy attacks.
The main contribution is a practical and scalable data usage estimator that could encourage further research in this area.
The paper is well motivated and addresses a gap in the literature by taking a fine grained approach to the data usage problem.
The proposed approach (DUCI) is significantly more computationally efficient compared to previous approaches.
This paper studies an interesting problem and proposes a new algorithm to predict a probability in [0,1] instead of {0,1} for the problem.
Though the authors proposed a specific algorithm, the technique here can be used for any algorithm that serves the purpose of membership query.
This paper is well-written and easy to read.
The authors also did experiments thoroughly by comparing with baselines and on different datasets.
weaknesses: There are approximations involved in deriving the confidence estimates, making them potentially incorrect.
Replacing $TPR_i$, $FPR_i$ with a single TPR/FPR across all samples, so the de-biasing is not exact.
Assuming independence of $\hat p_i$'s to compute the confidence intervals.

Using a single global TPR and FPR for debiasing each sample's membership score may introduce a bias if the true TPR and FPR vary significantly across different data points, especially when data points are not uniformly sampled or model performance varies across input space.

I would have liked to see some approaches for rigorously correct (asymptotic or non-asymptotic) confidence intervals in addition to the heuristic ones used here, e.g., XBern confidence intervals from [Pillutla et al] could be used.
I do not understand the derivation of footnote 1; it would be nice to expand on it (possibly in the supplement).
Figure 2 can be clearer if the x axis is in log scale.

Missing relevant references: [Kandpal et al] for membership inference of users (groups of data) and is related to dataset inference, [Vyas et al] for copyright protection, [Zhang et al.] for a recent MIA.

The presentation is vague; authors describe mathematical objects by vaguely saying what they are or make rushed arguments, which is not intuitive enough to give insight nor formal enough to have meaning.
It is unclear what is meant by “a number of population data” and what $\theta(x)_y$ denotes (as this is the first time they use this notation with y as a subscript).
It is unclear what the reference model is modelling, i.e., whether these models are for membership inference or represent a real world classifier or regressor.

The phrase “the probability of observing that i-th record’s likelihood to be a member is greater than randomly sampled population data points” is difficult to understand and seems irrelevant to the main contributions.

Dependence/correlation of records is handled in a confusing manner; the authors’ question “Will the ignorance of ‘correlations’ between records make our method sub-optimal?” is answered with “Yes”, but the paper does not clearly explain the need to divide the dataset into subgroups and de-bias using TPR/FPR within each subgroup.
The paper reads as if correlation between records is not an issue and that there is limited potential to improve their method in this regard, but this is not clearly stated.
It is unclear whether the assumptions underlying the MLE baselines (e.g., joint/mean logits follow a normal distribution) would not hinder the performance of these baselines.
The justification for presenting MLE with average logits as an idealized baseline is insufficient, despite its good performance in various experiments.
The method requires known training set for estimating FPR and TPR, but in practice the train set is usually private.
A comparison between DUCI and SOTA “binary” data usage algorithms for the specific case when p=1 and p=0 is missing, which would demonstrate comparable performance.
The technique seems quite simple and straightforward, raising doubts about the paper's contribution.
